# Sapporo Notes

## Overview

Five nights in Sapporo in the second month of the year, arriving by air from Tokyo and leaving by rail to the north coast. The city is laid out on a grid and easy to read, wider and calmer than the big island cities I knew. I stayed in a business hotel two blocks from the main station so that the underground walkway, which runs for kilometres beneath the centre, carried me everywhere without going outside. Days were short and bright, nights long and clear. I spent the first day simply walking the centre, learning the grid and finding the coffee shops that stayed open late. The pace here is unhurried and the food is generous, and I never once felt crowded except on the one evening I expected it. I paid 8500 yen a night for a compact room with a good bath, and the transport card from the airport covered the metro all week. I used the underground walkway for most errands, which kept me out of the wind and cost nothing. The clock tower and the old red-brick government building are close together and easy to see in an afternoon. The beer museum out of the centre makes a half-day trip, and the tram to the foot of the mountain runs past the ropes of the old town. The grid means a wrong turn is cheap to correct, and I learned my way within a day. I would happily return for a longer stay and use the city as a base for the coast and the hot springs to the south.

## Food

The eating in Sapporo is the reason I would return. The seafood is the headline: crabs, uni and salmon roe, and a bowl of rice topped with all three cost about 3500 yen at the market, worth every yen. The market hall near the station opens early and the stalls steam and grill from six in the morning, so I ate breakfast there twice. Miso ramen is the local bowl, thick and savoury, with a knob of butter and sweetcorn on top, and a large serving was 1100 yen at a counter near the hotel. I had it on three of the five evenings.

Soup curry is the other dish the city claims, a thin spiced broth with a whole chicken leg and heap of vegetables, and I ordered it twice at a basement shop, 1300 yen a bowl. Genghis Khan lamb, grilled at the table on a domed skillet, was the loudest and best meal of the trip, 3000 yen with drinks, and I left smelling of smoke. For a lighter lunch I bought a bento at the station for 700 yen and ate it on a bench in the snow-lined park. The soft-serve made with local milk was 400 yen and creamier than anything back home. Ramen alley under the station is a row of tiny counters and worth a look even if you eat elsewhere, and the queues are shortest just after opening. I tried the local cheese and the dried squid sold at the market, both cheap and both good with a beer.

## Notes

The cold is the thing nobody warns you about properly. It sat at minus 12 C for three of my five days, with a wind off the plain that cut through cloth, and I learned to respect it. I dressed in three layers under a down parka, a base of merino, a fleece and a shell, and I was fine as long as I kept moving. The insulated boots with a thick sole mattered more than the coat, because the pavement stays frozen and the cold comes up through thin soles. I carried hand warmers in a pocket and swapped them into my gloves at the halfway point of every walk. The ice sculptures along the main park are lit at night and worth the trip even at that temperature, though the crowds thicken after dark and the pathways turn to packed ice. I took the subway and chose the entrance nearest the hotel, a two-minute dash in the worst of the wind, which kept me warm between trains. If I packed again I would bring a second pair of gloves, a scarf wide enough to cover my face, and a smaller camera I could use without taking off a glove. I would leave the smart shoes at home and bring a spare hat. Two pairs of thick socks made more difference than I expected, because the ground holds the cold all day. I kept my phone in an inside pocket so the battery would last, since it drains fast in low temperatures. On the calmest morning I walked to the river and watched the mist sit over the water for an hour. The evenings after dark were busy around the main strip, with long queues at the food stalls and the sound of scraping ice underfoot. I would book a room with a bath again and spend one whole day indoors if the weather turned.
